title: (Scenario) The Terraform state file is accidentally deleted, or `terraform apply` fails midway leaving partially-created resources — how do you recover (state backup/versioning, `terraform import`, targeted apply)?
shortTitle: (Scenario) Terraform State Deleted or an Apply Fails Midway — How to Recover

s1_definition.profdef: These are two related disaster scenarios. If the state file is deleted, Terraform loses its map from configuration to real resources and will try to recreate everything, so recovery means restoring the state from a backup, typically S3 object versioning or a local backup, or if no backup exists, rebuilding the state with terraform import for each existing resource. If an apply fails midway, some resources were created and recorded while others were not, leaving a partial deployment; recovery means inspecting the state, re-running apply to continue from where it stopped, and using targeted apply or import to fix the specific resources that are inconsistent.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India the inventory ledger is how the bank knows which vault and ATMs it already owns. If the ledger is shredded, the bank might wrongly think it owns nothing and try to buy a second vault, so you restore the ledger from the head-office backup copy, or if there is no backup you physically walk the branch and re-enter each existing item into a fresh ledger. If a renovation is interrupted halfway, with the new counters installed but the ledger not yet updated, you compare what is physically there against the ledger and finish the job carefully, item by item, rather than restarting the whole renovation.
s1_definition.oneliner: Restore deleted state from S3 versioning or backup, or rebuild it with terraform import; for a half-finished apply, inspect state and re-run apply, using targeted apply and import to fix only the inconsistent resources.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** These are two related disaster scenarios. If the state file is deleted, Terraform loses its map from configuration to real resources and will try to recreate everything, so recovery means restoring the state from a backup, typically S3 object versioning or a local backup, or if no backup exists, rebuilding the state with terraform import for each existing resource. If an apply fails midway, some resources were created and recorded while others were not, leaving a partial deployment; recovery means inspecting the state, re-running apply to continue from where it stopped, and using targeted apply or import to fix the specific resources that are inconsistent.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India the inventory ledger is how the bank knows which vault and ATMs it already owns. If the ledger is shredded, the bank might wrongly think it owns nothing and try to buy a second vault, so you restore the ledger from the head-office backup copy, or if there is no backup you physically walk the branch and re-enter each existing item into a fresh ledger. If a renovation is interrupted halfway, with the new counters installed but the ledger not yet updated, you compare what is physically there against the ledger and finish the job carefully, item by item, rather than restarting the whole renovation.

**One line to remember:** Restore deleted state from S3 versioning or backup, or rebuild it with terraform import; for a half-finished apply, inspect state and re-run apply, using targeted apply and import to fix only the inconsistent resources.

sections.s2_technical:
The reason a deleted state is so dangerous is that the state is Terraform's only memory of what it created. Without it, Terraform compares the configuration against an empty state and concludes every resource must be created fresh, so the next apply would try to duplicate a production VPC, cluster, and database. The first and best recovery is to restore the state, which is exactly why remote state with S3 object versioning matters: every write creates a new object version, so a deleted or corrupted state can be restored by promoting a previous version. If you kept a local backup, Terraform also writes a terraform.tfstate.backup file on each apply that holds the prior state, which can rescue you locally.

If no backup exists at all, you rebuild the state by importing each real resource. terraform import takes a resource address from the configuration and the real cloud identifier and records the mapping into state without changing the resource. This is tedious because you import resources one by one and must know each real ID, but it fully reconstructs the state so Terraform stops wanting to recreate things. After importing, a plan should show no changes if the configuration matches reality.

A midway apply failure is different. Terraform applies resources in dependency order and records each success in state as it goes, so when apply fails partway, the resources created before the failure are real and tracked, while the failing resource and everything after it are not. Terraform usually reports exactly which resource failed and why. The primary recovery is simply to fix the cause, such as a quota limit, a bad input, or a transient API error, and run apply again; Terraform reads the state, sees what already exists, and continues from where it stopped rather than restarting. If the failing resource was left in a half-created, tainted condition, I can replace it on the next apply. If I want to proceed carefully and touch only specific resources, I use a targeted apply that limits the operation to a named resource or module, which is useful to repair one broken resource without risking the rest, though I treat targeting as a surgical tool rather than a normal workflow. If the failure created a real resource that never got recorded in state, that is untracked drift, and I use import to bring it under management so a retry does not duplicate it.

The senior discipline is prevention and calm procedure. I always use remote state with versioning and locking so a deletion is recoverable and concurrent applies cannot cause partial chaos, I never edit state by hand except as a last resort with the state commands, and I back up state before risky operations. When disaster strikes I resist the urge to run a blind apply, because an apply against a lost or inconsistent state can destroy or duplicate production resources. Instead I first restore or reconstruct the state, then run a plan to see exactly what Terraform intends, and only apply once the plan matches my understanding of reality. In a bank, that discipline is the difference between a quiet recovery and an outage.
sections.s3_banking:
At the National Bank of India both halves of this scenario happened, which is why we drilled the recovery.

Problem 1 — a cleanup script accidentally deleted the state object. Because the S3 bucket had versioning on, we restored the previous version and a plan immediately showed no changes, confirming recovery. Without versioning we would have had to import the VPC, cluster, and database by hand.

Problem 2 — an apply that was adding a new read-replica database failed midway because of a quota limit, after the networking was created but before the replica. Re-running apply after raising the quota continued from where it stopped, and a targeted apply let us repair just the replica without touching the healthy resources.

The mini-project is a runnable Java simulation of a `VersionedStateStore` that can be deleted and restored, a `StatefulApply` that records resources as it creates them and can fail midway, and a `Recovery` helper offering restore-from-version, import, and targeted apply. We delete the state and restore it, then fail an apply midway and recover, finally running a transfer for Rajesh and Priya on the recovered database.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile and run the recovery simulation
javac -d out sim/src/main/java/com/bank/recover/*.java
java -cp out com.bank.recover.RecoveryDemo

# Real Terraform recovery
# 1) Deleted state -> restore an S3 object version
aws s3api list-object-versions --bucket nbi-terraform-state --prefix prod/terraform.tfstate
aws s3api copy-object --copy-source "nbi-terraform-state/prod/terraform.tfstate?versionId=VER" \
  --bucket nbi-terraform-state --key prod/terraform.tfstate
terraform plan        # should show NO changes if restore matched reality
# 2) No backup -> rebuild via import
terraform import aws_db_instance.ledger ledger-db-id
# 3) Half-finished apply -> fix cause, then continue / target
terraform apply                              # continues from recorded state
terraform apply -target=aws_db_instance.replica   # repair only the broken resource
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a three-resource infrastructure, a state deletion, and a later expansion that fails midway.

Step 1 — The initial apply creates the VPC, cluster, and ledger database, recording each in state and saving a version. The state now knows all three resources exist.

Step 2 — Disaster one strikes: a script deletes the state object, so Terraform now believes nothing exists and would try to recreate everything, risking duplicate production resources.

Step 3 — Recovery restores the last good state version from S3 versioning. A follow-up apply reads the restored state, sees all three resources already present, and creates nothing, confirming a clean recovery with no duplicates. Had there been no backup, we would have imported each resource by real ID instead.

Step 4 — Disaster two strikes: an expansion applies a replica network and then a read-replica database, but the replica fails midway on a quota limit. The subnet was created and recorded, while the replica was not, leaving a partial state. The log shows the partial state containing the subnet but not the replica.

Step 5 — After raising the quota, a targeted apply repairs only the replica database without touching the healthy resources. With the infrastructure fully recovered, a transfer of fifty thousand rupees from Rajesh to Priya runs successfully on the ledger database.

sections.s5b_flow:
```
  apply → create VPC, EKS, ledger → record each → save version 1
    │
    ├─ DISASTER 1: state deleted
    │     │ Terraform thinks nothing exists (would duplicate!)
    │     ▼ restore S3 object version 1  (or: import each if no backup)
    │   plan → NO changes → recovered ✓
    │
    └─ DISASTER 2: apply expansion, FAIL midway at replica (quota)
          │ subnet recorded, replica NOT → partial state
          ▼ fix quota → apply continues from state
          ▼ apply -target=replica → repair ONLY replica
        recovered → transfer SAV2001→CUR3001 Rs.50000 ✓
  Rule: restore/rebuild state FIRST, plan, THEN apply — never blind apply.
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
These are two related disasters, and in both the single most important rule is to never run a blind apply, because an apply against a lost or inconsistent state can duplicate or destroy production resources. The state is Terraform's only memory of what it created, so I always recover or reconstruct the state first, run a plan to confirm what Terraform intends, and only apply once the plan matches reality.

If the state file is deleted, Terraform compares the configuration against an empty state and concludes it must create everything fresh, which in production means trying to build a second VPC, cluster, and database. The best recovery is to restore the state, which is exactly why I keep remote state in a versioned S3 bucket: every write is a new object version, so I promote the last good version and a follow-up plan should show no changes, confirming the restore matched reality. Locally, Terraform also writes a backup state file on each apply that can rescue me. If there is no backup at all, I rebuild the state with terraform import, taking each resource address and its real cloud identifier to record the mapping without changing the resource, which is tedious but fully reconstructs the state so Terraform stops wanting to recreate things.

If an apply fails midway, Terraform applies in dependency order and records each success as it goes, so the resources before the failure are real and tracked while the failing one and everything after it are not, leaving a partial deployment. The primary recovery is to fix the root cause, such as a quota limit or a bad input, and simply run apply again, because Terraform reads the state, sees what already exists, and continues from where it stopped rather than restarting. If I want to be surgical, I use a targeted apply to repair only the broken resource without risking the healthy ones, and if the failure created a real resource that never got recorded, I import it so a retry does not duplicate it.

In my project at the National Bank of India both happened. A cleanup script deleted the state object, but because the bucket had versioning on, we restored the previous version and a plan immediately showed no changes. And an expansion that added a read-replica failed midway on a quota limit after the networking was created, so once we raised the quota we re-ran apply to continue and used a targeted apply to repair just the replica without touching the healthy resources. The discipline I carry from that is that remote state with versioning and locking turns a potential outage into a calm, procedural recovery, and the order is always restore or rebuild the state, plan, then apply, never apply first.
